The hybrid absorber (HA) achieves a minimum reflection loss of –22 dB at 8.9 GHz.
The dielectric composite absorber is fabricated with graphite and glass microballoon powders mixed into epoxy resin.
Sample C1 with 75% graphite and 25% GMB shows the widest 10 dB absorption bandwidth of 1.5 GHz at 1.2 mm thickness.
The metamaterial unit cell is a hexagonal closed ring with arrows, designed for electric and magnetic resonance.
The HA structure layers: 2 mm aluminum sheet, 0.5 mm FR-4 substrate with metamaterial, and 1.2 mm dielectric composite absorber.
The dielectric constant of composite C1 ranges from 7.5 to 6.8 in 6–12 GHz, with loss tangent 0.85 to 1.1.
The absorption bandwidth of the HA with C1 composite and metamaterial is 6 GHz at 1.2 mm thickness.
The antenna used for testing is a wideband Vivaldi antenna operating from 6 to 12 GHz.
The HA reduces the in-band radar cross section (RCS) of the antenna significantly while preserving antenna gain and radiation pattern.
The admittance analysis shows the real part of HA admittance close to free space admittance (~2.65 × 10⁻³ S) and imaginary part near zero.
The dielectric composite is fabricated by mixing epoxy LY5052 and hardener HY5052 in 100:38 ratio, stirred at 500 rpm, sonicated for 25 minutes, and cured under vacuum at 50°C for 2 hours.
Graphite powder average particle size is 10 μm; glass microballoon average diameter is 20 μm.
The metamaterial unit cell achieves a reflection minimum of –19.51 dB at 9.74 GHz with 200 MHz bandwidth.
The surface current distribution in the metamaterial shows circulating currents creating magnetic resonance.
The HA concept combines dielectric composite and metamaterial to broaden absorption bandwidth while minimizing thickness.
The dielectric absorber alone has reflection loss between –2 to –12 dB in 6–12 GHz, improved to –12 to –25 dB when combined with metamaterial.
The hybrid absorber is suitable for aerospace and stealth applications due to its lightweight and broadband absorption.
The fabricated dielectric composite sheet dimensions are 15 cm × 15 cm for free-space measurements.
The reflection loss (RL) is calculated using normalized input impedance and S-parameters measured experimentally.
The metamaterial structure is simulated using CST Microwave Studio with periodic boundary conditions and plane wave excitation.
